title: Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

    Title:Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely studied for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where its advantage estimator assigns each rollout a magnitude from within-group reward statistics. In the common case, this magnitude rewards rollouts that reach the correct answer through reasoning. Yet, an overlooked case shares the same surface: a rollout may land on it by guessing, and the formula still assigns a high magnitude, which we identify as the spurious advantage. This arises in three cases: bounded-answer tasks with a small candidate set; open-answer sets hosting bounded sub-cases; and search agents whose budget opens many paths to the same answer. In all three, this misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors. We propose SIGNBALANCE, whose magnitude is composition-free: it keeps the verifier sign, uses a global scale, and restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales, SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves on bounded-answer math and search agents. Code will be released.

report.summary: GRPO can reward lucky guesses, not true reasoning; SIGNBALANCE fixes spurious advantages and beats GRPO on bounded math and search tasks.
report.background: GRPO has become a standard method for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards in large language models. It estimates an advantage for each rollout by comparing its reward with group-level statistics: rollouts whose reward is above the group average get a positive advantage. The intended signal is to reinforce those rollouts that reach a correct answer via sound reasoning. However, GRPO's estimator only observes the final verifier outcome, not the reasoning process itself. Consequently, a rollout that reaches the correct answer by pure guessing receives the same high-magnitude advantage as one produced through valid derivation. This “spurious advantage” is especially likely in bounded-answer tasks with small candidate sets, open-ended tasks containing bounded sub-cases, and agentic search settings where large budgets generate many attempts that happen to land on the same correct answer. The proposed SIGNBALANCE method attempts to restore accurate credit assignment by separating the sign of the verifier from a globally scaled magnitude and applying per-class rescaling with stop-gradient updates to keep advantages zero-mean without leaking class information.
key_points: GRPO's advantage estimator compares rollouts within a group using reward statistics. It is meant to favor reasoning that reaches a correct verifier reward. But the advantage is based solely on final answer correctness, not on how the answer was obtained. Thus guesses that happen to match a correct label receive the same positive advantage as genuinely reasoned solutions.

Spurious advantage appears in three situations: tasks with limited candidate answers, open-ended answer sets that contain small bounded sub-cases, and agentic search settings where a large budget generates many candidate paths to the same answer. These contexts inflate the chance that a random or shallow rollout lands on a correct-looking final result.

The paper proposes SIGNBALANCE as a fix. Instead of a within-group magnitude built from reward composition, it uses a global scale for magnitude, keeps the verifier sign for direction, and applies per-class rescaling via stop-gradient to maintain zero-mean advantage while avoiding class leakage. This separates quality signal from accidental answer coverage.

Experiments show SIGNBALANCE performs on par with GRPO on open-ended mathematical reasoning, but yields improvements on bounded-answer math tasks and on search agent benchmarks. These are exactly the areas where spurious advantage should bias GRPO, suggesting the method addresses the root cause while retaining strengths on open-answer tasks.
report.impact: For the AI community, this paper exposes a silent failure mode in GRPO-style training: models may be learning guess-like heuristics rather than robust reasoning, particularly when verifiable answers are drawn from small sets. SIGNBALANCE offers a more truthful credit-assignment mechanism that preserves GRPO's strengths while reducing spurious reinforcement. Developers using RL with verifiable rewards should audit their tasks for bounded-answer spaces or budget-heavy search pipelines. The method also matters for regular users, since models trained without spurious advantage should show fewer shallow shortcut behaviors and more reliable reasoning. As verifier-based RL becomes increasingly common for math, code, and agentic models, correcting these biases could translate into better generalisation, less reward hacking, and more trustworthy outputs across real deployments.
report.tools: Watch for the promised SIGNBALANCE code release on the authors’ page and arXiv. For those working with GRPO today, open-source implementations in Hugging Face TRL, verl, and OpenRLHF offer convenient baselines to replicate spurious-advantage tests. Agentic search evaluation can be explored with frameworks such as LangGraph or DSPy, while math reasoning benchmarks like MATH500, GSM8K, and AIME can help probe bounded-answer behavior.
